Empirical Research Plan – “Does Banking Deregulation Promote Economic Growth?”

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Strategy: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimated with modern “interaction-weighted” estimators (Sun & Abraham, 2020; Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021), complemented by an event-study to trace dynamics and by a synthetic-control robustness check for early– versus late-adopters.

Why appropriate:
• Deregulation is an absorbing, one-time policy whose timing varies by state (1970-94).  
• We observe pre- and post-outcomes annually for all states.  
• Institutional accounts suggest timing was largely political rather than driven by contemporaneous growth.  
• Modern staggered-DiD estimators avoid bias that can arise in two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) with heterogeneous treatment effects.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable
   Treat_it = 1 if state i has fully removed intrastate branching restrictions by year t; 0 otherwise. The variable is “absorbing”: once 1, always 1.

Control group
   In any year t the controls are states that have not yet deregulated (Treat_it = 0). Because states join treatment at different times, each treated state is compared to the “not-yet-treated” cohort in that year.

Timing / variation
   Key variation is the adoption year DeregYear_i. Event-time indicators k = –6,…,+10 (with k = –1 omitted) allow us to estimate leads/lags:

   Y_it = Σ_k≠–1 β_k · 1(EventTime_it = k) + α_i + γ_t + ε_it

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: Absent deregulation, treated and not-yet-treated states would have evolved similarly.  
     Plausibility: Many macro forces are national; still, states differ. We will test for pre-trends, add state-specific linear trends, and control for time-varying covariates.

A2. No anticipatory effects: Economic growth does not change in anticipation of future deregulation.  
     Plausibility: Branching laws typically changed quickly after passage; we will inspect β_k in the –6 … –2 window.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): One state’s deregulation does not directly alter another’s growth path.  
     Plausibility: Possible spillovers through regional credit markets; we will probe by excluding neighbours or adding neighbour-treatment dummies.

A4. Exogeneity of adoption timing: Conditional on fixed effects and controls, deregulation timing is unrelated to unobserved growth shocks.  
     Plausibility: Political narratives support exogeneity; we will instrument timing with political variables in robustness checks.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Endogenous timing (states deregulate when their economy slows):  
   • Add state-specific linear (or flexible spline) trends.  
   • Include lagged growth rates as controls.  
   • Instrument adoption year with political variables (party control, legislative term limits).

T2. Spillovers / credit migration across state lines:  
   • Drop states whose neighbours deregulated earlier (“buffer sample”).  
   • Include average treatment of bordering states as an additional regressor; coefficient should be small.

T3. Heterogeneous dynamic effects biasing TWFE:  
   • Use SA- or CS-weighted estimator instead of simple TWFE.  
   • Report group-specific ATTs by adoption cohort.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# Required packages
library(data.table)      # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)          # high-dimensional FE regressions
library(did)             # Callaway & Sant’Anna staggered-DiD
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
dat <- fread("state_panel_1972_1992.csv")   # Assume wide file with all variables

# 2. Variable construction
dat[, treat := ifelse(year >= dereg_year, 1, 0)]      # absorbing treatment
dat[, rel_year := year - dereg_year]                  # event time
# Collapse extreme leads/lags
dat[rel_year < -6, rel_year := -6]
dat[rel_year > 10, rel_year := 10]

# 3. Main specification – Callaway & Sant’Anna estimator
cs_res <- att_gt(yname = "log_gsp_percap",  # outcome
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "state",
                 gname = "dereg_year",      # first treated period, NA for never treated
                 xformla = ~ educ + urban + industry_share,
                 data = dat,
                 panel = TRUE)

agg_cs   <- aggte(cs_res, type = "group")   # overall ATT
event_cs <- aggte(cs_res, type = "dynamic") # event-study

# 4. TWFE comparison (Sun & Abraham)
dat[, factor_rel := factor(rel_year)]
sa_res <- feols(log_gsp_percap ~ i(rel_year, treat, -1) + educ + urban + industry_share | state + year, 
                data = dat, cluster = "state")

# 5. Robustness: drop border states with early-dereg neighbours
border_pairs <- fread("state_borders.csv")   # adjacency matrix long form
dat[, early_neigh := any(treat[ match(border_pairs[border_pairs$state1==state, state2], state) ] == 1), by = .(state, year)]
robust_dat <- dat[early_neigh == 0]
robust_cs  <- att_gt(yname = "log_gsp_percap", tname = "year",
                     idname = "state", gname = "dereg_year",
                     data = robust_dat, panel = TRUE)

# 6. Plot dynamic effects
event_df <- data.frame(year = as.numeric(names(event_cs$att.egt)),
                       att = event_cs$att.egt,
                       se = event_cs$se.egt)
ggplot(event_df, aes(x = year, y = att)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = att - 1.96*se, ymax = att + 1.96*se), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1, lty = 2) +
  labs(title = "Event-study: Intrastate Branch Deregulation and GSP per capita",
       x = "Years relative to deregulation", y = "ATT (log points)")
```

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Theory predicts a positive effect: branching freedom boosts competition, lowers lending rates, and reallocates capital more efficiently, raising productivity. Prior work on liberalisation of interstate banking finds ~0.3–0.5 pp faster annual income growth. For intrastate branching — arguably a smaller but still meaningful shock — I expect 0.15–0.30 percentage-point higher growth, cumulating to ≈3–6 % higher per-capita income after 10 years.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = good, 0 = weak)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(1) Clear shock / quasi-experiment………………… 1  
(2) Plausible parallel trends (pre-trend tests)……… 0.8  
(3) No anticipation……………………………………… 0.8  
(4) No spillovers / SUTVA……………………………… 0.7  
(5) Measurement accuracy of treatment & outcome…… 1  

Overall: 4.3 / 5 – credible but hinges on demonstrating parallel trends and limited spillovers.
